application.cover_letter_markdown:
What drew me to the Senior Signal Processing Engineer opening at Kaikuvaara Oy was the measurement and characterisation angle that I gathered from the job description. My background is in RF measurement rather than algorithm development or system design, and I want to be upfront about that, but I think there may be enough overlap to make this worth a conversation.

I've been at Polaris RF Labs in Espoo for most of my career – since January 2014, with a sabbatical year in 2016–17. My day-to-day work is running antenna measurement campaigns. I handle everything from fixture design through to final reporting: setting up prototypes in the anechoic chamber, running S-parameter sweeps and pattern measurements on PNA-X and ZVA network analysers, processing the near-field data, and compiling the results into technical reports for customers. It's hands-on lab work and I've become very comfortable with it over the years.

My degree is in Industrial Management from Tammerkoski University, which I know is not the conventional background for this kind of role. The path was somewhat accidental – I did a summer placement at Polaris during my studies, helping set up measurement equipment in the lab, and they offered me a position after graduation. The RF measurement work turned out to suit me and I stuck with it. Over ten years I've built up practical knowledge that I couldn't have got from coursework, even if the theoretical foundations are something I've had to pick up along the way rather than study formally.

Since coming back from the sabbatical I've taken on more of the complex measurement campaigns – broadband prototypes where the fixture design needs custom work and the coupling paths are tricky to account for. Those projects have been the most educational. But at Polaris my responsibilities have stayed relatively static overall. It's a small lab team and the work is cyclical.

The sabbatical in 2016–17 was something I'd planned for a while. I spent eight months travelling through Thailand, Vietnam, and Laos, then three months in Peru and Bolivia. When I got back, I returned to the same role at Polaris and picked things up again fairly quickly. The fundamentals of the measurement work hadn't changed, though the lab had some new equipment that took time to learn.

I'm applying to Kaikuvaara because I'd like my next step to involve more than what I currently do. I don't have exposure to the broader signal processing challenges that Kaikuvaara seems to work on, and I'm realistic about the gap between what I do now and what this role probably requires. But I'm willing to learn, and the measurement side of things is one area where I could contribute from the start.

I hold a Finnish permanent residence permit and have been in Finland since 2013. I'm based in Espoo but would happily relocate to Oulu – I've moved before for work and have no particular ties to the capital region.

I've attached my CV and am available to discuss the role at your convenience.

Sanne Kovac

application.cover_letter_markdown:
Oulu's concentration of RF and photonics companies has caught my attention over the past few years. I attended the Arctic Sensors Workshop there in 2022 and again in 2024, and both times came away thinking that the signal processing work happening in the region is genuinely interesting at a scale I haven't seen elsewhere in northern Europe. Kaikuvaara's posting for a Senior Signal Processing Engineer is what finally made me put together a formal application.

I have been at Nordkom Radar Systems in Hamburg since 2004, which is a long time in one place. The reason is prosaic: the work kept changing even though the company didn't. I started on the coastal surveillance radar line, moved through vessel traffic management variants, and have spent the last several years on the newest generation of the X-band platform. But two decades at one employer means I also know what I haven't done, and I haven't worked on the kinds of systems Kaikuvaara builds. That gap is part of the appeal.

My formal background is an MSc in Electrical Engineering from Rheinmark TU Aachen (2003), where my thesis covered adaptive beamforming under barrage jamming conditions – a constrained least-squares formulation that I ended up adapting for Nordkom's first digital beamformer the following year. That academic starting point in array signal processing has stayed directly relevant to everything I've worked on since.

I have team leadership experience from several periods at Nordkom. Regarding publications, I have three papers in ISRT Radar, Sonar & Navigation – two on adaptive beamforming methods and one on detection performance in heavy sea clutter – and I presented at the Baltic Radar Conference in Barcelona in 2018. Not a huge body of academic work, but each paper came out of problems I'd spent serious time working through at Nordkom rather than from a pressure to publish.

I hold German citizenship and can work anywhere in the EU without restrictions.

I should be straightforward about what's missing from my profile. Twenty years at a single maritime radar company means my experience is deep but narrow in terms of application domain. I've never worked on the kinds of systems that Kaikuvaara appears to build, and I don't know your specific toolchains or delivery model. My belief is that the signal processing fundamentals and the phased-array experience transfer cleanly, but I'd be the first to admit there would be a learning curve on the domain side.

I think there is enough here to be worth a conversation, and I hope the application gives you enough to consider one.

Leila Sharma

application.cover_letter_markdown:
After fourteen years at Meridian Defence Electronics, I'm looking for a change. Not because the work itself has gone stale – the HAR-6 programme I was on most recently was technically the best project of my career – but because Meridian's reorganisation has shifted the Stockholm DSP group away from new development and towards sustainment of delivered systems. I'd rather keep building things.

My background is array signal processing. I wrote my MSc thesis at RRIT on wideband spatial filtering, and everything I've done since at Meridian has been radar signal processing in one form or another – ground surveillance, airborne GMTI, electronic warfare support. What I've enjoyed most has been work where I follow a problem from initial algorithm design through embedded implementation into field validation.

Kaikuvaara's posting describes the kind of engineering environment I'm looking for: a phased-array-focused company, small enough that the distance between algorithm design and deployed hardware is short. At Meridian I've watched that distance grow as the organisation has layered programme management between the engineering teams and actual system integration. I don't want to spend the next decade writing reports about algorithms that someone else implements.

What I bring is fairly specific. I've designed and built adaptive beamformers, written embedded DSP firmware running in real time on multi-core processors, built production test infrastructure, and characterised RF hardware in chamber and field environments. I've done this across multiple radar programmes, on systems that have been delivered and are in operational use. The profile is narrow but deep.

What I don't bring: I have never worked outside defence. Defence customers operate on long cycles with heavy documentation overhead, and I have no idea whether that maps to Kaikuvaara's delivery model. I'd expect some adjustment period.

I also want to be direct about what I'm looking for. This isn't a speculative application. I've been thinking about leaving Meridian for the better part of a year, and the only openings that interest me are ones where phased-array signal processing is the core work. Kaikuvaara is one of a very small number of companies in the Nordics doing that at a serious level, which is why I'm writing.

If the profile looks like a plausible fit, I'm available to talk at your convenience.

Diego Souza

application.cover_letter_markdown:
I graduated from Tammerkoski University last year with an MSc in Electrical Engineering and have been working at Polaris RF Labs since January. That makes me junior for a senior position, I know, and I'm applying anyway because the technical fit between my experience and what Kaikuvaara does seems closer than my years of experience alone would suggest.

The specific overlap is in phased-array signal processing. At Polaris, the satellite communication terminal I work on uses a 16-element planar phased array for tracking LEO satellites across the sky. I've been responsible for the beam-steering implementation – computing pointing weights from orbital prediction data and applying them in real time during satellite passes. The accuracy requirements are tight because LEO pass durations are short and the handover between satellites needs to be seamless. Most of the algorithm work was prototyped in MATLAB, but the deployed version runs on a TI C6748 DSP, and I wrote the C implementation of the beam-steering controller including the weight computation loop and the SPI interface to the RF front-end module.

Oulu's RF and photonics engineering cluster has been on my radar since my thesis years at Tampere. Several companies in the region work on problems adjacent to satellite communication, but Kaikuvaara's focus on phased-array systems specifically is what sets it apart. I've been following the company for a while and the chance to work on larger, more complex arrays than the 16-element terminal I deal with at Polaris would be a genuine step forward technically.

One thing I can offer despite limited post-university experience is a track record of writing code that gets used. The Python test framework I built at Polaris runs every night and has caught real bugs. The embedded C code for the beam-steering controller runs in the field. I co-authored a paper that went through peer review and was presented at BALSIPCO. None of this is the scale of accomplishment you'd get from a candidate with ten years of experience, obviously, but it's real work and I think it shows I can deliver.

What I lack is breadth. I've been at one employer. The systems I've worked on are small compared to what Kaikuvaara probably builds, and I haven't been through a full product development cycle from requirements through to field deployment. I'd be bringing strong fundamentals in a narrow area rather than broad industrial experience.

Whether that's enough for a senior role is your call. I wouldn't normally apply for a position at this level, but the alignment between the phased-array and embedded DSP work I do now and what this role requires seemed too close to pass up without trying. If you're open to hearing from a less experienced candidate with directly relevant recent work, I'd appreciate the chance to speak with you.

Tomi Korhonen

Livia Berg
livia.berg@mail.example | +358 00 000 0165

EXPERIENCE

Sumuvire Wireless, Oulu
Signal Processing Engineer | 2006 – present

Develop and maintain real-time DSP firmware in C for Sumuvire’s wireless transceiver product line, running on ARM Cortex-M4 and TI C5000 series processors. Primary responsibility for the baseband processing chain: timing synchronisation, channel estimation, equalisation. Over the past few years I have also been involved in receiver architecture design for Sumuvire’s next-generation wideband transceiver.

Hold a Finnish permanent residence permit (EU long-term residence status, obtained 2012). Based in Oulu since joining Sumuvire in 2006.

EDUCATION

Sakura National University
MSc Applied Physics, 2005
Thesis: “Finite-difference time-domain modelling of electromagnetic wave propagation in structured urban environments”

PROJECTS

4-Element Beamforming Demonstrator (personal project, 2023)
Built a small phased-array beamforming setup at home using four microstrip patch antenna elements at 2.4 GHz on a custom PCB, with individual RF phase shifters controlled via an Arduino Mega. Implemented a delay-and-sum beamformer and measured the resulting patterns using a makeshift rotary positioner in my garage. Element spacing was set at half-wavelength based on first-principles calculations. Measured roughly 8 dB directional gain relative to a single element, with beam steering across about ±30 degrees before grating lobes became significant. The calibration process — compensating for element-to-element phase and amplitude mismatch — turned out to be the most difficult part and was done iteratively with a signal generator and oscilloscope. Not production-quality by any measure, but useful for building intuition about array calibration and weight computation.

MSc Thesis Work (Sakura National University, 2004–2005)
My master’s research in applied physics involved modelling RF wave propagation through urban geometries using FDTD methods. The simulation framework required validation against analytically solvable cases, which gave me a working understanding of electromagnetic field behaviour, antenna radiation characteristics, and numerical methods for wave equations. The physics and mathematics from this work have been directly applicable to the transceiver signal path design I’ve done at Sumuvire over the past two decades.

SKILLS

- Python: built automated production test scripts at Sumuvire for transceiver board-level validation (pytest, pySerial, NumPy); scripts run as part of manufacturing acceptance and are used on every board
- RF measurement: regular use of spectrum analysers (R&S FSW), signal generators (Keysight E8267D), and oscilloscopes for transceiver development, characterisation, and debugging
- Languages: English (working language at Sumuvire since 2010, when international customer contracts started), Finnish (intermediate), Japanese (conversational from university years)
- Location: based in Oulu since 2006; no relocation needed
application.cover_letter_markdown:
I’ve lived in Oulu for twenty years now and have watched the RF engineering community here change shape — from what was mostly Korvenmaa legacy into something broader and more varied. Sumuvire Wireless has been a good employer through all of that, but the signal processing problems at a small transceiver company are bounded, and after nearly two decades I know where the ceiling is. Kaikuvaara works on things I haven’t been able to do at Sumuvire, and the fact that I wouldn’t need to uproot my life to take the job is a practical advantage worth stating plainly.

My career at Sumuvire has been long and narrowly focused. I joined in 2006 after finishing my MSc at the Sakura National University in applied physics, and the work has always centred on single-channel transceiver baseband processing — synchronisation, equalisation, receiver firmware. It’s solid work and I’m good at it, but the problems I solve now are refinements of problems I solved a decade ago.

What draws me to Kaikuvaara is the shift from single-channel to array-based systems. I’ve been curious about spatial signal processing for a while and have explored it on my own time — enough to appreciate how large the gap is between a hobby experiment and a production multi-element system. The real learning happens on the production side, and I’d like to be there.

I know the Oulu engineering ecosystem well. I attend Suvanto’s sensor workshops, I know people at several of the local companies, and I follow the work coming out of the university’s CRSR group. Kaikuvaara’s growth over the past few years has been visible from within the community, and the word is that you do genuine array work rather than consultancy. That matters.

The practical side is simple: I live here already, my family is here, and I have no interest in relocating. If the technical fit works, the logistics are trivial.

I should be honest about what might give you pause. Twenty years at one small company means depth in a narrow domain. My formal training is in applied physics, not electrical engineering, and the array work I’ve done is self-directed. Whether that profile is enough for what you need is a fair question, and I’d rather discuss it in person than argue it in a letter.

Livia Berg

Outi Salo
outi.salo@mail.example | +358 00 000 0166

Experience

Kajanti Avionics, Oulu
Signal Processing Engineer | 2012 – present

Joined Kajanti after completing my PhD in physics at the Merihaka University. The statistical signal detection and spectral analysis methods from my doctoral research have been directly applicable to Kajanti’s radar sensor processing work throughout my time here. Currently based at the Oulu site.

Education

Merihaka University
PhD Physics, 2011
Dissertation: “Statistical methods for weak signal detection in broadband electromagnetic spectra”

Projects

Analysis Tooling
During my PhD I wrote a set of data analysis scripts to automate processing of large experimental datasets — spectral decomposition, statistical hypothesis testing, batch visualisation. When I moved to Kajanti, I adapted these tools for sensor test campaign data. Over the years the codebase grew well beyond what I’d originally intended: automated report generation, a test vector library for regression validation, overnight batch scheduling, and a database backend (PostgreSQL) for archiving processed results. The stack is built on NumPy, SciPy, and matplotlib, with a Flask interface for submitting jobs and reviewing outputs. What started as one physicist’s convenience scripts is now the analysis pipeline the entire signal processing group uses for test data reduction.

Ground Radar Sensor RF Characterisation (2019–2020)
Led a team of four engineers through a 14-month characterisation campaign for Kajanti’s ground-based radar sensor module. Planned the test matrix, coordinated chamber scheduling and equipment allocation, assigned measurement tasks, and compiled the final characterisation report. The campaign covered S-parameter measurements, noise figure characterisation, and gain flatness assessment across temperature, using Rohde & Schwarz ZNB VNA and calibrated noise source equipment.
Finnish citizen, EU work authorisation.

Skills

- Embedded C/C++: real-time DSP algorithm implementation on TI C6748 and Xilinx Zynq SoC for Kajanti’s sensor processing boards; fixed-point FFT and detection threshold logic running under FreeRTOS with deterministic timing constraints
- MATLAB/Simulink for algorithm prototyping and system modelling
- Statistical signal detection theory
application.cover_letter_markdown:
Signal processing for phased-array systems is where I want my career to go next, and that means leaving Kajanti Avionics.

I’ve spent fourteen years at Kajanti in Oulu doing sensor-level signal processing. The physics PhD gave me a strong foundation in statistical detection theory and spectral analysis, and I’ve applied those methods daily — designing detection algorithms, building analysis infrastructure, running characterisation campaigns. But the work has been overwhelmingly single-channel, and after this long the technical ceiling is real.

That changed earlier this year when I was brought onto a customer project involving a 32-element receive array for a ground-based surveillance application. I designed the digital beamforming pipeline from scratch: spatial covariance estimation, adaptive weight computation, beam pattern verification against predicted performance. I also built the array calibration procedure, mapping measured element patterns to steering vector corrections. Those eight months were the most technically demanding and engaging of my career at Kajanti, and they made it obvious that phased-array work is what I want as my main focus.

Kaikuvaara is the obvious next step. It’s the company in Oulu — in Finland, really — where array-based signal processing is core business rather than a sideline. Going from Kajanti, where array work surfaces as an occasional customer request, to somewhere it’s the daily work is exactly the shift I need.

I’m also comfortable with Kalman filtering and estimation theory, though my recent applied work has been mostly on the detection side.

My CV reads as weighted toward physics and sensor-level work, and it is. But the signal processing fundamentals carry across — spatial filtering, adaptive algorithms, calibration, embedded implementation — and the move from single-channel to array processing is one I’ve already started. I’d like to complete it at Kaikuvaara.

I’m in Oulu already. No relocation involved.

Outi Salo

Johanna Saarinen
johanna.saarinen@mail.example | +358 00 000 0167

Education

TU Maasdelta
MSc Electrical Engineering, 2018
Specialisation: signal processing and wireless communications

Experience

Meridian Defence Electronics, Gothenburg
Signal Processing Engineer | January 2019 – present

Signal processing algorithm development for Meridian’s ground-based surveillance radar programmes. Applied the signal processing and communications theory from my MSc directly to radar waveform design, detection algorithms, and receiver chain development from the start.

Finnish citizen, EU work authorisation.

Career break | September 2021 – August 2022
Caregiving leave.

Projects

GS-200 Digital Receiver (2022 – present)
Main assignment since returning from leave. The GS-200 is a ground-based surveillance radar with a 48-element UHF phased-array antenna.

- Designed the phased-array beamforming pipeline: calibration data management, steering vector computation, adaptive null placement for interference rejection, and beam scheduling logic
- Wrote the embedded C++ implementation running on TI C6678 multi-core DSP hardware, with real-time constraints requiring careful memory management and pipeline scheduling across four cores
- Built the production Python regression testing framework for the GS-200 beamformer: automated test vector generation from recorded field data, golden reference comparison, pass/fail reporting, and GitLab CI integration; the framework runs nightly and defect reports feed into the programme’s tracking system

Planned relocation
Currently in Gothenburg. My partner and I are relocating to Oulu — we have family in the region and want to return to Finland. Available from late 2026.

Interests

Cross-country skiing, trail running
application.cover_letter_markdown:
Two things make this application unusual: I finished my MSc only eight years ago, and there’s a year-long caregiving gap in the middle. I’m applying for a senior role anyway because the work I’ve done since returning from leave in 2022 has been at exactly the level this posting describes.

The GS-200 programme at Meridian is where it came together for me. Since late 2022 I’ve owned the digital beamforming chain on a 48-element ground surveillance radar — algorithm design through real-time embedded implementation on multi-core DSP hardware. It’s the kind of assignment where you touch every layer of the processing chain and carry end-to-end responsibility for whether the beamformer actually works in the field. That concentration of experience in three focused years has been worth more, I’d argue, than a longer career spent on smaller slices of bigger programmes, though I’m aware that’s easy to say from the inside.

One aspect that doesn’t show well in my CV is the RF measurement work tied to the GS-200. I spent roughly three months at Meridian’s near-field scanning facility characterising the UHF antenna array — running element pattern measurements on a Kuusela Scanning planar scanner, extracting mutual coupling coefficients, and building the calibration tables the beamformer depends on. I operated Rohde & Schwarz ZVA67 network analysers, designed measurement fixtures for sub-array mounting, and was responsible for the test plan, execution scheduling, and the final calibration dataset.

I should note that English has been my working language for the past decade. The team at Meridian in Gothenburg is international, and all technical documentation, design reviews, and customer reporting happen in English. My MSc at TU Maasdelta was also taught and examined entirely in English. Finnish is my first language, but I’ve worked in English professionally since leaving Finland for university.

The move to Oulu is happening regardless of this specific application. My partner and I have been planning it for over a year — we have family in the region and want our children to grow up in Finland. But the alignment between what Kaikuvaara does and what I’ve spent the past three years building at Meridian is closer than I expected to find anywhere. Ground-based phased-array radar is a narrow field and there aren’t many companies in the Nordics doing it at this level, which is why I’m writing to you rather than casting a wider net.

I recognise the caregiving gap and the modest total years are unusual for a senior position. I’d rather let you weigh that against the depth of the GS-200 work than try to argue past it in a letter. If the profile looks interesting, I’d welcome a conversation.

Johanna Saarinen

WEI PATEL
wei.patel@mail.example | +39 00 000 0168

PROFILE

Signal processing engineer with background in phased-array systems and RF characterisation. Led a team of six DSP engineers as Head of DSP at Polaris RF Labs, driving algorithm development and system validation for active antenna products. Experience with satellite and airborne platform integration.

EDUCATION

Politecnico del Naviglio
MSc Telecommunications Engineering, 2021

EXPERIENCE

Polaris RF Labs, Tampere
Signal Processing Engineer | March 2022 – present

- Develop phased-array beamforming algorithms for Polaris’s 24-element S-band active antenna module: steering vector computation, sidelobe suppression, and array calibration
- Applied MIMO channel estimation methods from my MSc research at Politecnico del Naviglio to phased-array calibration and beamformer design at Polaris
- Conduct RF characterisation of antenna elements and sub-arrays using Keysight N5224B PNA network analyser and near-field scanning in Polaris’s anechoic chamber
- Parental leave: July 2024 – June 2025

PROJECTS

Relocation
Based in Tampere. Willing to relocate to Oulu; have attended Suvanto workshops in the region and am familiar with the local technology cluster.

SKILLS

- Python: developed automated beamformer validation and regression testing tools using NumPy, SciPy, and pytest; integrated with Jenkins CI for nightly runs across Polaris’s DSP team
- Satellite and airborne platform experience
- MATLAB/Simulink
- Git, JIRA
application.cover_letter_markdown:
Polaris RF Labs brought me to Finland from Italy in 2022, and the phased-array work I’ve done since has confirmed that the Nordic RF engineering scene is where I want to build my career. Kaikuvaara’s focus on array-based systems is the closest match to my background that I’ve found outside my current employer.

The embedded implementation side of my work is what I want to highlight here. At Polaris I wrote the real-time beamforming controller in C for a TI C6748 DSP — a fixed-point pipeline handling steering weight computation and application at frame rate, with hard real-time constraints and no FPU. The inner loop had to meet a 1 ms budget per beam update, requiring hand-optimised memory access patterns and arithmetic. I also developed the C++ host interface for calibration data management and configuration. That embedded DSP work has been the most technically demanding part of my time at Polaris.

I published a first-authored paper in 2023: W. Patel et al., ‘Calibration error compensation for planar phased arrays under near-field conditions,’ at the SESE International Symposium on Phased Array Systems and Technology. Based on measurement data from Polaris’s S-band module, fully peer-reviewed. I presented it at the conference in Boston and intend to keep contributing to the field.

I hold Italian citizenship and have unrestricted EU work authorisation. I’ve been living and working in Finland on that basis since 2022.

Oulu’s RF and photonics cluster is part of what makes this move appealing. I attended the Arctic Sensors Workshop there last year and was struck by the concentration of radar and array-focused companies in one city. Kaikuvaara has a strong reputation within that community for the ambition and scale of its phased-array work.

I took parental leave from mid-2024 to mid-2025. Since coming back I’ve been weighing my options. Polaris has been a good start to my career in Finland, but it’s a small company and the array work I can do there is limited by product scale. The 24-element module is interesting but I want to work on larger, more demanding systems. Kaikuvaara is where that work happens, and I’d relocate to Oulu without hesitation.

Wei Patel
